desc:
A hiker studies a rectangular map where heights[r][c] is the altitude of cell (r, c). The hiker starts at the top-left cell (0, 0) and wants to reach the bottom-right cell, moving one step at a time up, down, left or right.

The effort of a route is the largest absolute difference in altitude between two consecutive cells on it, not the total. Return the smallest effort among all routes from the top-left cell to the bottom-right cell. If both cells are the same cell, the effort is 0.
constraints: All rows have the same length
hints: Walking cheaply is not the goal. What counts for a route is its single worst step, so you want to minimise a maximum, not a sum.
Either guess an effort limit x and check whether the goal is reachable using only steps of difference at most x (the limit is monotone, so binary search works), or tweak Dijkstra's algorithm.

In Dijkstra, let the cost of reaching a cell be the minimum possible effort of any route to it. Moving to a neighbour gives max(cost_here, |height difference|); keep the usual min-heap and relax when that value improves.
editorial: This is a shortest path problem with a different way of combining edge weights: the cost of a route is the maximum of its edge weights (a bottleneck path). Dijkstra's algorithm still works because extending a route can never lower its cost. Store the best known effort per cell, start with 0 at the top-left, and always pop the cell with the smallest effort. For each neighbour compute max(effort, |h[a] - h[b]|) and push it if it beats the neighbour's best. The first time the bottom-right cell is popped, its effort is optimal. The cost is O(R · C · log(R · C)).

Alternatives: binary search on the effort limit with a BFS feasibility test costs O(R · C · log(max height)); or sort all adjacent-cell edges by difference and add them with union-find until the two corners become connected. They all return the same value.
